<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D01:9" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Errors

Every error response has the same shape:

```json
{"error": {"code": "REG-1007", "name": "MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED", "message": "claude-opus is not allowed on tier standard"}}
```

The `code` is stable and safe to match on in code; the `message` is for people and may change. The full list is in the error code reference.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:1" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > How to instrument" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## How to instrument

The short answer is to instrument everything. Every library, subsystem and
service should have at least a few metrics to give you a rough idea of how it is
performing.

Instrumentation should be an integral part of your code. Instantiate the metric
classes in the same file you use them. This makes going from alert to console to code
easy when you are chasing an error.
</source>

Check its status first: someone may have paused it, or it may have hit a spending cap. Then check whether it's on a model that's being switched off. </source>

### Metamonitoring

It is important to have confidence that monitoring is working. Accordingly, have
alerts to ensure that Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, PushGateways, and
other monitoring infrastructure are available and running correctly.

As always, if it is possible to alert on symptoms rather than causes, this helps
to reduce noise. For example, a blackbox test that alerts are getting from
PushGateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than individual
alerts on each.

monitoring can catch problems that are otherwise invisible, and also serves as
a fallback in case internal systems completely fail.

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:8" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Metamonitoring" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Metamonitoring

It is important to have confidence that monitoring is working. Accordingly, have
alerts to ensure that Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, PushGateways, and
other monitoring infrastructure are available and running correctly.

As always, if it is possible to alert on symptoms rather than causes, this helps
to reduce noise. For example, a blackbox test that alerts are getting from
PushGateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than individual
alerts on each.

Supplementing the whitebox monitoring of Prometheus with external blackbox
monitoring can catch problems that are otherwise invisible, and also serves as
a fallback in case internal systems completely fail.
</source>

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="D01:9" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Errors

Every error response has the same shape:

```json
{"error": {"code": "REG-1007", "name": "MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED", "message": "claude-opus is not allowed on tier standard"}}
```

The `code` is stable and safe to match on in code; the `message` is for people and may change. The full list is in the error code reference.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

<source id="D02:2" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Limits and availability" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Limits and availability

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1009` | `RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | The key made too many requests this minute. Wait the number of seconds in `Retry-After`, then retry. |
| `REG-1011` | `REGISTRY_READ_ONLY` | 503 | The registry is in maintenance mode. Reads work; writes are refused until maintenance ends. |
</source>

<source id="D14:0" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?

Check its status first: someone may have paused it, or it may have hit a spending cap. Then check whether it's on a model that's being switched off. If it's running but every task fails, look at the errors in its logs. An error code starting with `REG-` comes from the registry, and the error code reference explains each one.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

<source id="D01:9" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Errors

Every error response has the same shape:

```json
{"error": {"code": "REG-1007", "name": "MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED", "message": "claude-opus is not allowed on tier standard"}}
```

The `code` is stable and safe to match on in code; the `message` is for people and may change. The full list is in the error code reference.
</source>

## How to instrument

The short answer is to instrument everything. Every library, subsystem and
service should have at least a few metrics to give you a rough idea of how it is
performing.

Instrumentation should be an integral part of your code. Instantiate the metric
classes in the same file you use them. This makes going from alert to console to code
easy when you are chasing an error.
</source>

<source id="D14:0" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?

Check its status first: someone may have paused it, or it may have hit a spending cap. Then check whether it's on a model that's being switched off. If it's running but every task fails, look at the errors in its logs. An error code starting with `REG-` comes from the registry, and the error code reference explains each one.

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D08:1" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Alerts" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Alerts

| Alert | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `AgentLatencyHigh` | p95 response time above 8 seconds for 10 minutes |
| `AgentErrorRateHigh` | more than 5% of sessions end in an error over 15 minutes |
| `RegistryUnreachable` | three registry polls in a row fail (`MON-2002`) |

Alerts go to the on-call channel and page the on-call engineer between 08:00 and 20:00. Outside those hours, only `RegistryUnreachable` pages.
</source>

Metrics in layperson terms is a standard for measurement. What we want to measure depends from application to application. For a web server it can be request times, for a database it can be CPU usage or number of active connections etc.

| Labels | KV | A set of labels to be attached to the alert. |

| StartsAt | time.Time | The time the alert started firing. If omitted, the current time is assigned by the Alertmanager. |
| EndsAt | time.Time | Only set if the end time of an alert is known. Otherwise set to a configurable timeout period from the time since the last alert was received. |
| GeneratorURL | string | A backlink which identifies the causing entity of this alert. |
| Fingerprint | string | Fingerprint that can be used to identify the alert. |
</source>

# Annotations to add to each alert.

## Defining alerting rules

The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to wait for a certain duration
between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting
an alert as firing for this element. In this case, Prometheus will check that
the alert continues to be active during each evaluation for 10 minutes before
firing the alert. Elements that are active, but not firing yet, are in the pending state.
Alerting rules without the `for` clause will become active on the first evaluation.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

</source>

## Requirements of HTTP SD endpoints

The whole list of targets must be returned on every scrape. There is no support
for incremental updates. A Prometheus instance does not send its hostname and it
is not possible for a SD endpoint to know if the SD requests is the first one
after a restart or not.

The URL to the HTTP SD is not considered secret. The authentication and any API
keys should be passed with the appropriate authentication mechanisms. Prometheus
supports TLS authentication, basic authentication, OAuth2, and authorization
headers.

## Requirements of HTTP SD endpoints

The whole list of targets must be returned on every scrape. There is no support
for incremental updates. A Prometheus instance does not send its hostname and it
is not possible for a SD endpoint to know if the SD requests is the first one
after a restart or not.

The URL to the HTTP SD is not considered secret. The authentication and any API
keys should be passed with the appropriate authentication mechanisms. Prometheus
supports TLS authentication, basic authentication, OAuth2, and authorization
headers.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

## When to rotate

Rotate an agent's registry key every 90 days, and immediately if the key may have been exposed: written to a log, pasted in a chat, or committed to a repository. An exposed key is rotated first and investigated second.
</source>

<source id="D06:3" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 3: Verify" date="2026-07-20" type="official">

</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

## What the platform is

The agent platform is the set of services our agents run on. Agents are configured in the registry, look things up through shared services, and are watched by monitoring. This page describes the core services and how they connect. It doesn't cover every service an individual agent uses; each agent's owner documents those.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

<source id="D08:2" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > When RegistryUnreachable fires" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## When RegistryUnreachable fires

Check the registry's status page first. While the registry is down, monitoring can't refresh its agent list, so dashboards may show no agents at all even though the agents are still running. Don't read an empty dashboard as "every agent is down."
</source>

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D03:2" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.4 — 2026-05-12" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.4 — 2026-05-12

- Lowered the rate limit from 100 to 60 requests per minute per key. Some internal dashboards were polling hard enough to slow the registry for agents.
- Rate-limited responses (`REG-1009`) now include a `Retry-After` header.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D01:2" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Listing agents" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Listing agents

`GET /agents` returns agents in pages. Pass `limit` to set the page size (default 20, maximum 100). Each response includes a `next_cursor`; pass it back as `cursor` to get the next page. When `next_cursor` is `null`, there are no more pages.

```bash
curl "https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents?limit=50&cursor=eyJpZCI6IDUwfQ" \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

```json
{
  "agents": [
    {"agent_id": "support_agent", "model": "claude-sonnet", "tier": "standard", "status": "active"}
  ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IDEwMH0"
}
```

You can filter by `status` (`active`, `paused` or `retired`) and by `owner`.
</source>

## Packaging and dependencies

Ideally, a client library can be included in any application to add some
instrumentation without breaking the application.

Accordingly, caution is advised when adding dependencies to the client library.
For example, if you add a library that uses a Prometheus client that requires
version x.y of a library but the application uses x.z elsewhere, will that have
an adverse impact on the application?

It is suggested that where this may arise, that the core instrumentation is
separated from the bridges/exposition of metrics in a given format. For
example, the Java simpleclient `simpleclient` module has no dependencies, and
the `simpleclient_servlet` has the HTTP bits.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

<source id="D04:3" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > The agents that use them" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## The agents that use them

`support_agent` answers customer questions. It looks up agent and account configuration through registry-api and searches help articles through kb-search. `triage_agent` reads incoming tickets and hands the ones it can't close to `support_agent`.
</source>

<source id="D04:4" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Who to contact" date="2026-02-14" type="official">

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

    histogram_fraction(0, 0.2, rate(http_request_duration_seconds[1h]))

The error of the estimation depends on the resolution of the underlying native
histogram and how closely the provided boundaries are aligned with the bucket
boundaries in the histogram.

`+Inf` and `-Inf` are valid boundary values. For example, if the histogram in
the expression above included negative observations (which shouldn't be the
case for request durations), the appropriate lower boundary to include all
observations less than or equal 0.2 would be `-Inf` rather than `0`.

## `info()`

If there is no matching info series for a given time series in `v` at a
particular timestamp (e.g. because the info series has gone stale), the
behavior depends on the data label matchers: If the `data-label-selector`
contains any matcher that does not match the empty string (e.g.
`{data=~".+"}`), then that time series is dropped from the result at that
timestamp, because the required enrichment is unavailable. If all matchers
match the empty string (e.g. `{data=~".*"}`), or if no `data-label-selector`
is provided, the time series is returned without enrichment.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:27" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `histogram_fraction()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `histogram_fraction()`

Whether the provided boundaries are inclusive or exclusive is only relevant if
the provided boundaries are precisely aligned with bucket boundaries in the
underlying native histogram. In this case, the behavior depends on the schema
definition of the histogram. (The usual standard exponential schemas all
feature inclusive upper boundaries and exclusive lower boundaries for positive
values, and vice versa for negative values.) Without a precise alignment of
boundaries, the function uses interpolation to estimate the fraction. With the
resulting uncertainty, it becomes irrelevant if the boundaries are inclusive or
exclusive.
</source>

RENAME` does not disconnect users, which in most cases will go unnoticed, though might in some cases cause a program confusion if it depends in some way upon database name.

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D14:2" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > How do I find out which model my agent is on?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">

</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}

## Root cause

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:26" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `histogram_fraction()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `histogram_fraction()`

    histogram_fraction(0, 0.2, rate(http_request_duration_seconds[1h]))

The error of the estimation depends on the resolution of the underlying native
histogram and how closely the provided boundaries are aligned with the bucket
boundaries in the histogram.

`+Inf` and `-Inf` are valid boundary values. For example, if the histogram in
the expression above included negative observations (which shouldn't be the
case for request durations), the appropriate lower boundary to include all
observations less than or equal 0.2 would be `-Inf` rather than `0`.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:49" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `info()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `info()`

If there is no matching info series for a given time series in `v` at a
particular timestamp (e.g. because the info series has gone stale), the
behavior depends on the data label matchers: If the `data-label-selector`
contains any matcher that does not match the empty string (e.g.
`{data=~".+"}`), then that time series is dropped from the result at that
timestamp, because the required enrichment is unavailable. If all matchers
match the empty string (e.g. `{data=~".*"}`), or if no `data-label-selector`
is provided, the time series is returned without enrichment.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:27" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `histogram_fraction()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `histogram_fraction()`

Whether the provided boundaries are inclusive or exclusive is only relevant if
the provided boundaries are precisely aligned with bucket boundaries in the
underlying native histogram. In this case, the behavior depends on the schema
definition of the histogram. (The usual standard exponential schemas all
feature inclusive upper boundaries and exclusive lower boundaries for positive
values, and vice versa for negative values.) Without a precise alignment of
boundaries, the function uses interpolation to estimate the fraction. With the
resulting uncertainty, it becomes irrelevant if the boundaries are inclusive or
exclusive.
</source>

Running `DROP DATABASE` or `ALTER DATABASE ... SET TABLESPACE` on the primary will generate a WAL entry that will cause all users connected to that database on the standby to be forcibly disconnected. RENAME` does not disconnect users, which in most cases will go unnoticed, though might in some cases cause a program confusion if it depends in some way upon database name.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D04:4" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Who to contact" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Who to contact

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

## Why and by when

<source id="D14:0" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?

Check its status first: someone may have paused it, or it may have hit a spending cap. Then check whether it's on a model that's being switched off. If it's running but every task fails, look at the errors in its logs. An error code starting with `REG-` comes from the registry, and the error code reference explains each one.
</source>

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

#### Planning for High Availability

In a priority-based synchronous replication, the standbys whose names appear earlier in the list will be used as synchronous standbys. Standbys listed after these will take over the role of synchronous standby if one of current ones should fail.

In a quorum-based synchronous replication, all the standbys appearing in the list will be used as candidates for synchronous standbys. Even if one of them should fail, the other standbys will keep performing the role of candidates of synchronous standby.
</source>

- Queued tickets accumulated as agents couldn't transfer work to other agents
- On-call engineers were paged due to the outage notification

In summary, a registry-db failure creates a cascading impact across agent functionality, monitoring visibility, operational dashboards, and ticket management workflows.

Based on the documentation and incident records, when **registry-db fails**, the following systems are affected:

## Direct Impact on System Components
- **registry-api** can't answer at all [D04:2]
- **Monitoring** loses sight of every agent for the outage duration [D11:0] - it gets its agent list from registry-api every 30 seconds
- **All agents** that need to look things up in the registry can't complete their tasks [D11:0]

## Agent-Specific Impacts (from INCIDENT INC-2093)
During a past registry-db failure where api was unavailable for 42 minutes:

| Agent | Impact |
|-------|--------|
| **support_agent** | Sessions failed on their first registry lookup; now tells users registry is unavailable instead of failing silently [D11:3, D11:1] |
| **triage_agent** | Kept running but couldn't hand tickets over → **212 tickets queued** [D11:1] |
| **Overview dashboard** | Went blank because it shows no agent list [D11:1] |

## Teams Affected
- **support-team**: Their `support_agent` (customer questions) and `triage_agent` ticket flow interrupted
- **research-team**: Their `research_agent` would be unable to complete tasks requiring registry lookups
- **finance-team**: Their `billing_agent` similarly affected if it needs registry access

The most severe impact was operational: during the last incident, the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected because monitoring showed nothing. The fix now is that monitoring keeps the last good agent list, and an alert fires when standby falls more than 60 seconds behind [D11:3].

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:23" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Data Checksums > Online Enabling of Checksums > Impact on System of Online Operations" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Impact on System of Online Operations

Enabling data checksums can cause significant I/O to the system, as all of the database pages will need to be rewritten, and will be written both to the data files and the WAL. The impact may be limited by throttling using the `cost_delay` and `cost_limit` parameters of the `pg_enable_data_checksums()` function.

- I/O: all pages need to have data checksums calculated and written which will generate a lot of dirty pages that will need to be flushed to disk, as well as WAL-logged.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/instrumenting/writing_clientlibs.md:7" doc="prometheus-docs/instrumenting/writing_clientlibs.md" title="Writing client libraries" section="Writing client libraries > Metrics" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Metrics

This will register requests with the default CollectorRegistry. By calling
`build()` rather than `register()` the metric won’t be registered (handy for
unittests), you can also pass in a CollectorRegistry to `register()` (handy for
batch jobs).
</source>

<source id="D10:2" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Why it took a week to notice" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/instrumenting/writing_clientlibs.md:6" doc="prometheus-docs/instrumenting/writing_clientlibs.md" title="Writing client libraries" section="Writing client libraries > Metrics" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Metrics

There MUST be a default CollectorRegistry, the standard metrics MUST by default
implicitly register into it with no special work required by the user. There
MUST be a way to have metrics not register to the default CollectorRegistry,
for use in batch jobs and unittests. Custom collectors SHOULD also follow this.

Exactly how the metrics should be created varies by language. For some (Java,
Go) a builder approach is best, whereas for others (Python) function arguments
are rich enough to do it in one call.

For example in the Java Simpleclient we have:

```java
class YourClass {
  static final Counter requests = Counter.build()
      .name("requests_total")
      .help("Requests.").register();
}
```
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager > Grouping" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.
</source>

Based on the documentation and incident records, when **registry-db fails**, the following systems are affected:

## Direct Impact on System Components
- **registry-api** can't answer at all [D04:2]
- **Monitoring** loses sight of every agent for the outage duration [D11:0] - it gets its agent list from registry-api every 30 seconds
- **All agents** that need to look things up in the registry can't complete their tasks [D11:0]

## Agent-Specific Impacts (from INCIDENT INC-2093)
During a past registry-db failure where api was unavailable for 42 minutes:

| Agent | Impact |
|-------|--------|
| **support_agent** | Sessions failed on their first registry lookup; now tells users registry is unavailable instead of failing silently [D11:3, D11:1] |
| **triage_agent** | Kept running but couldn't hand tickets over → **212 tickets queued** [D11:1] |
| **Overview dashboard** | Went blank because it shows no agent list [D11:1] |

## Teams Affected
- **support-team**: Their `support_agent` (customer questions) and `triage_agent` ticket flow interrupted
- **research-team**: Their `research_agent` would be unable to complete tasks requiring registry lookups
- **finance-team**: Their `billing_agent` similarly affected if it needs registry access

The most severe impact was operational: during the last incident, the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected because monitoring showed nothing. The fix now is that monitoring keeps the last good agent list, and an alert fires when standby falls more than 60 seconds behind [D11:3].

<source id="prometheus-docs/instrumenting/writing_clientlibs.md:6" doc="prometheus-docs/instrumenting/writing_clientlibs.md" title="Writing client libraries" section="Writing client libraries > Metrics" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Metrics

There MUST be a default CollectorRegistry, the standard metrics MUST by default
implicitly register into it with no special work required by the user. There
MUST be a way to have metrics not register to the default CollectorRegistry,
for use in batch jobs and unittests. Custom collectors SHOULD also follow this.

Exactly how the metrics should be created varies by language. For some (Java,
Go) a builder approach is best, whereas for others (Python) function arguments
are rich enough to do it in one call.

For example in the Java Simpleclient we have:

```java
class YourClass {
  static final Counter requests = Counter.build()
      .name("requests_total")
      .help("Requests.").register();
}
```
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager > Grouping" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.
</source>

Based on the documentation and incident records, when **registry-db fails**, the following systems are affected:

## Direct Impact on System Components
- **registry-api** can't answer at all [D04:2]
- **Monitoring** loses sight of every agent for the outage duration [D11:0] - it gets its agent list from registry-api every 30 seconds
- **All agents** that need to look things up in the registry can't complete their tasks [D11:0]

## Agent-Specific Impacts (from INCIDENT INC-2093)
During a past registry-db failure where api was unavailable for 42 minutes:

| Agent | Impact |
|-------|--------|
| **support_agent** | Sessions failed on their first registry lookup; now tells users registry is unavailable instead of failing silently [D11:3, D11:1] |
| **triage_agent** | Kept running but couldn't hand tickets over → **212 tickets queued** [D11:1] |
| **Overview dashboard** | Went blank because it shows no agent list [D11:1] |

## Teams Affected
- **support-team**: Their `support_agent` (customer questions) and `triage_agent` ticket flow interrupted
- **research-team**: Their `research_agent` would be unable to complete tasks requiring registry lookups
- **finance-team**: Their `billing_agent` similarly affected if it needs registry access

The most severe impact was operational: during the last incident, the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected because monitoring showed nothing. The fix now is that monitoring keeps the last good agent list, and an alert fires when standby falls more than 60 seconds behind [D11:3].

Based on my analysis of your incidents and documentation, here are the recurring causes that appear across incidents:

## Common Incident Patterns:

**1. Unmonitored Service Dependencies Failures**
- *Example*: INC-2041 - **expired intermediate certificate in auth-service** caused payment gateway timeouts [D09:2]
- Pattern: Critical service dependencies fail without triggering alerts, leading to cascading failures

**2. Hidden Data Quality Issues**
- *Example*: INC-2067 - **cached outdated results** appeared normal in metrics but were wrong [D10:2]
- Pattern: Agents show healthy error rates and latencies while serving stale or incorrect data; monitoring only captures surface metrics

**3. Infrastructure Drift & Latency Problems**
- *Example*: INC-2093 - **standby server fell 38 minutes behind** during failover, no alerts triggered for this lag [D11:2]
- Pattern: Infrastructure components drift over time; alerting doesn't detect these slow degradation paths

**4. Monitoring Blind Spots**
- Common theme across all three incidents: standard monitoring metrics (error rate, response time) masked the actual root cause
- The registry itself was unmonitored in INC-2093 since its agent list depends on the registry creating a blind spot
- Content freshness wasn't being validated in INC-2067 despite looking "healthy"

## Summary:
The most frequent recurring issue is **relying on traditional health metrics (latency, errors) without validating the actual correctness or state of services**. When you see "normal" error rates but unexpected behavior occurs, it's often because:
- A dependency failed silently (certificate expiry)
- Cached/stale data looks good but isn't useful (research_agent)
- Infrastructure drifted past the point of detection thresholds (database failover lag)

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D10:2" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Why it took a week to notice" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

**1. Unmonitored Service Dependencies Failures**

Based on my investigation of your incident log and documentation, here are the recurring patterns and root causes I found:

## Recurring Causes Across Incidents

### 1. **Configuration Drift & Approval Process Gaps**
**INC-2067**: A cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days without proper approval. The Search team's review process wasn't exercised, allowing an inappropriate configuration to go live that persisted for a week [D10:3].

**Pattern**: Configuration changes affecting core services sometimes bypass proper change review, particularly for operational parameters like caching, timeouts, and retry behavior.

### 2. **Missing Alerts on Failure Modes**
**INC-2093**: During database failover, nothing alerted on the standby falling 38 minutes behind the primary, resulting in a 42-minute outage instead of a brief 5-minute transition [D11:2].

**INC-2041**: There was no pre-existence alert for certificate expiration, only a post-incident fix to add a 30-day advance warning [D09:3].

**Pattern**: Key infrastructure failure modes (lag between replicas, certificate expiration, cache staleness) aren't automatically monitored or detected until user-facing impact occurs.

### 3. **Service Dependency Cascades**
**INC-2041**: auth-service certificate expiry → payments-gateway timeout (due to bad error handling) → billing_agent excessive retries → session failures [D09:1].

**Pattern**: Downstream services don't properly handle upstream service degradation. The payments-gateway should have returned an immediate error instead of timing out.

### 4. **Monitoring Blind Spots**
**INC-2067**: Latency and error metrics looked fine because cached answers were fast and never failed, but there was no monitoring for data currency/quality [D10:2].

**INC-2093**: When the registry went down, monitoring lost sight of every agent because the agent list comes from the registry itself, creating a feedback loop [D11:2].

---

**Summary**: Your most common recurring causes involve **misconfigurations going unreviewed**, **infrastructure failure modes lacking visibility through monitoring gaps**, **service dependencies failing gracefully**, and **monitoring blind spots where systems can't see themselves**.

#### Failures

Failures should be handled similarly to logging. Every time there is a failure, a
counter should be incremented. Unlike logging, the error may also bubble up to a
more general error counter depending on how your code is structured.

When reporting failures, you should generally have some other metric
representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

content.text:
Based on my investigation of your incident log and documentation, here are the recurring patterns and root causes I found:

## Recurring Causes Across Incidents

### 1. **Configuration Drift & Approval Process Gaps**
**INC-2067**: A cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days without proper approval. The Search team's review process wasn't exercised, allowing an inappropriate configuration to go live that persisted for a week [D10:3].

**Pattern**: Configuration changes affecting core services sometimes bypass proper change review, particularly for operational parameters like caching, timeouts, and retry behavior.

### 2. **Missing Alerts on Failure Modes**
**INC-2093**: During database failover, nothing alerted on the standby falling 38 minutes behind the primary, resulting in a 42-minute outage instead of a brief 5-minute transition [D11:2].

**INC-2041**: There was no pre-existence alert for certificate expiration, only a post-incident fix to add a 30-day advance warning [D09:3].

**Pattern**: Key infrastructure failure modes (lag between replicas, certificate expiration, cache staleness) aren't automatically monitored or detected until user-facing impact occurs.

### 3. **Service Dependency Cascades**
**INC-2041**: auth-service certificate expiry → payments-gateway timeout (due to bad error handling) → billing_agent excessive retries → session failures [D09:1].

**Pattern**: Downstream services don't properly handle upstream service degradation. The payments-gateway should have returned an immediate error instead of timing out.

### 4. **Monitoring Blind Spots**
**INC-2067**: Latency and error metrics looked fine because cached answers were fast and never failed, but there was no monitoring for data currency/quality [D10:2].

**INC-2093**: When the registry went down, monitoring lost sight of every agent because the agent list comes from the registry itself, creating a feedback loop [D11:2].

---

**Summary**: Your most common recurring causes involve **misconfigurations going unreviewed**, **infrastructure failure modes lacking visibility through monitoring gaps**, **service dependencies failing gracefully**, and **monitoring blind spots where systems can't see themselves**.

Would you like me to look up more specific details about any of these patterns, or help you draft action items addressing them?

#### Failures

Failures should be handled similarly to logging. Every time there is a failure, a
counter should be incremented. Unlike logging, the error may also bubble up to a
more general error counter depending on how your code is structured.

When reporting failures, you should generally have some other metric
representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.
</source>

### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

Based on my investigation of your incident log and documentation, here are the recurring patterns and root causes I found:

## Recurring Causes Across Incidents

### 1. **Configuration Drift & Approval Process Gaps**
**INC-2067**: A cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days without proper approval. The Search team's review process wasn't exercised, allowing an inappropriate configuration to go live that persisted for a week [D10:3].

**Pattern**: Configuration changes affecting core services sometimes bypass proper change review, particularly for operational parameters like caching, timeouts, and retry behavior.

### 2. **Missing Alerts on Failure Modes**
**INC-2093**: During database failover, nothing alerted on the standby falling 38 minutes behind the primary, resulting in a 42-minute outage instead of a brief 5-minute transition [D11:2].

**INC-2041**: There was no pre-existence alert for certificate expiration, only a post-incident fix to add a 30-day advance warning [D09:3].

**Pattern**: Key infrastructure failure modes (lag between replicas, certificate expiration, cache staleness) aren't automatically monitored or detected until user-facing impact occurs.

### 3. **Service Dependency Cascades**
**INC-2041**: auth-service certificate expiry → payments-gateway timeout (due to bad error handling) → billing_agent excessive retries → session failures [D09:1].

**Pattern**: Downstream services don't properly handle upstream service degradation. The payments-gateway should have returned an immediate error instead of timing out.

### 4. **Monitoring Blind Spots**
**INC-2067**: Latency and error metrics looked fine because cached answers were fast and never failed, but there was no monitoring for data currency/quality [D10:2].

**INC-2093**: When the registry went down, monitoring lost sight of every agent because the agent list comes from the registry itself, creating a feedback loop [D11:2].

---

**Summary**: Your most common recurring causes involve **misconfigurations going unreviewed**, **infrastructure failure modes lacking visibility through monitoring gaps**, **service dependencies failing gracefully**, and **monitoring blind spots where systems can't see themselves**.

### Scope

Graphite focuses on being a
passive time series database with a query language and graphing features. Any
other concerns are addressed by external components.

Prometheus is a full monitoring and trending system that includes built-in and
active scraping, storing, querying, graphing, and alerting based on time series
data. It has knowledge about what the world should look like (which endpoints
should exist, what time series patterns mean trouble, etc.), and actively tries
to find faults.

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md:9" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md" title="The Zen of Prometheus" section="The Zen of Prometheus > If you can log it, you can have a metric for it" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## If you can log it, you can have a metric for it

Logs are often critical for troubleshooting, but metrics are equally valuable—a troubleshooting journey typically jumps back and forth between different signals. Don't underestimate the value of metrics for understanding what is going on.

Whenever you log an event, consider counting it by broad category. This is cheap and gives you alerting on elevated error rates plus an overview of what is happening. Remember, a metric without labels is cheap—spread counters liberally.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md:15" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md" title="The Zen of Prometheus" section="The Zen of Prometheus > Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

For more context My Philosophy on Alerting.
</source>

## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.

### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.

## If you can log it, you can have a metric for it

Logs are often critical for troubleshooting, but metrics are equally valuable—a troubleshooting journey typically jumps back and forth between different signals. Don't underestimate the value of metrics for understanding what is going on.

Whenever you log an event, consider counting it by broad category. This is cheap and gives you alerting on elevated error rates plus an overview of what is happening. Remember, a metric without labels is cheap—spread counters liberally.

## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

For more context My Philosophy on Alerting.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours.
