<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

smoothed value for each float time series in the range in `v`. The lower the
smoothing factor `sf`, the more importance is given to old data. The higher the

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:33" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Common Pitfalls" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:12" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > How to instrument > Subsystems > Failures" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
#### Failures

Failures should be handled similarly to logging. Every time there is a failure, a
counter should be incremented. Unlike logging, the error may also bubble up to a
more general error counter depending on how your code is structured.

When reporting failures, you should generally have some other metric
representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:27" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Cluster Size Considerations" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Cluster Size Considerations

Since Alertmanager uses gossip without quorum or voting, **any N instances tolerate up to N-1 failures** - as long as one instance is alive, notifications will be sent.

However, cluster size involves tradeoffs:

**Benefits of more instances:**
- Greater resilience to simultaneous failures (hardware, network, datacenter outages)
- Continued operation even during maintenance windows

**Costs of more instances:**
- In case of partitions there will be an increase in duplicate notifications
- More gossip traffic

**Typical deployments:**
- **2-3 instances** - Common for single-datacenter production deployments
- **4-5 instances** - Multi-datacenter or highly critical environments
</source>

### Batch jobs

For batch jobs it makes sense to page if the batch job has not succeeded
recently enough, and this will cause user-visible problems.

This should generally be at least enough time for 2 full runs of the batch job.
For a job that runs every 4 hours and takes an hour, 10 hours would be a
reasonable threshold. If you cannot withstand a single run failing, run the
job more frequently, as a single failure should not require human intervention.
</source>

## When does it fit?

Prometheus works well for recording any purely numeric time series. It fits
both machine-centric monitoring as well as monitoring of highly dynamic
service-oriented architectures. In a world of microservices, its support for
multi-dimensional data collection and querying is a particular strength.

Prometheus is designed for reliability, to be the system you go to
during an outage to allow you to quickly diagnose problems. Each Prometheus
server is standalone, not depending on network storage or other remote services.
You can rely on it when other parts of your infrastructure are broken, and
you do not need to set up extensive infrastructure to use it.

### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings

answers:
Based on the incidents we've reviewed, our monitoring has exposed several critical gaps:

## 1. **Complete Blind Spots During Infrastructure Events**

**INC-2093 - Registry Outage (42 minutes)** [D11:0]
- **Gap**: Monitoring relied entirely on the registry for the agent list, so when the registry was unreachable, the overview dashboard went completely blank
- **Impact**: On-call engineer had zero visibility into which agents were affected during the outage
- **Root cause**: The monitoring lost sight of every agent; its agent list comes from the registry and there was no alert on the standby falling 38 minutes behind

## 2. **Stale-Correct Behavior Without Detection**

**INC-2067 - Research Agent Serving Outdated Results** [D10:0]
- **Gap**: No automated alert fired because the agent itself functioned correctly (no errors occurred)
- **Impact**: User discovered four days later that answers contained policies changed just before they were cached
- **Root cause**: kb-search cache TTL was misconfigured from 7 hours to 7 days

## 3. **Timing-Based Alert Blindness**

**INC-2041 - Billing Agent Invoicing Failures** [D09:0]
- **Gap**: Error rate alert fired but it was "outside paging hours" so nobody saw it immediately
- **Impact**: 1,140 invoices went out late before on-call engineer arrived
- **Root cause**: Payments-gateway timeouts from expiring certificates were treated as transient and retried repeatedly

## 4. **Upstream Failure Detection Gap**

In INC-2041, monitoring could only detect downstream timeouts, not the root cause:
- Auth-service intermediate certificate had expired at 06:00
- Payments-gateway checked and failed, then timed out instead of returning an error
- Monitoring never alerted to certificate expiration or auth-service health

## Summary of Gaps Identified:
| Gap Type | Example | What We Changed |
|----------|---------|-----------------|
| Lost agent visibility | INC-2093: blank dashboard | Keep last good agent list when registry unreachable |
| Missing lag alerts | INC-2093: 38-min catch-up gap | Fire alert when standby >60s behind |
| Silent staleness | INC-2067: no alerts at all | Need content freshness monitoring |
| Timing blindness | INC-2041: outside paging hours | Ensure coverage across all hours |
| Upstream detection | INC-2041: cert expiry unknown | Monitor upstream service dependencies |

### Administrator's Overview

Advisory locks work normally in recovery, including deadlock detection. Note that advisory locks are never WAL logged, so it is impossible for an advisory lock on either the primary or the standby to conflict with WAL replay. </source>

## Summary

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the incidents we've reviewed, our monitoring has exposed several critical gaps:

## 1. **Complete Blind Spots During Infrastructure Events**

**INC-2093 - Registry Outage (42 minutes)** [D11:0]
- **Gap**: Monitoring relied entirely on the registry for the agent list, so when the registry was unreachable, the overview dashboard went completely blank
- **Impact**: On-call engineer had zero visibility into which agents were affected during the outage
- **Root cause**: The monitoring lost sight of every agent; its agent list comes from the registry and there was no alert on the standby falling 38 minutes behind

## 2. **Stale-Correct Behavior Without Detection**

**INC-2067 - Research Agent Serving Outdated Results** [D10:0]
- **Gap**: No automated alert fired because the agent itself functioned correctly (no errors occurred)
- **Impact**: User discovered four days later that answers contained policies changed just before they were cached
- **Root cause**: kb-search cache TTL was misconfigured from 7 hours to 7 days

## 3. **Timing-Based Alert Blindness**

**INC-2041 - Billing Agent Invoicing Failures** [D09:0]
- **Gap**: Error rate alert fired but it was "outside paging hours" so nobody saw it immediately
- **Impact**: 1,140 invoices went out late before on-call engineer arrived
- **Root cause**: Payments-gateway timeouts from expiring certificates were treated as transient and retried repeatedly

## 4. **Upstream Failure Detection Gap**

In INC-2041, monitoring could only detect downstream timeouts, not the root cause:
- Auth-service intermediate certificate had expired at 06:00
- Payments-gateway checked and failed, then timed out instead of returning an error
- Monitoring never alerted to certificate expiration or auth-service health

## Summary of Gaps Identified:
| Gap Type | Example | What We Changed |
|----------|---------|-----------------|
| Lost agent visibility | INC-2093: blank dashboard | Keep last good agent list when registry unreachable |
| Missing lag alerts | INC-2093: 38-min catch-up gap | Fire alert when standby >60s behind |
| Silent staleness | INC-2067: no alerts at all | Need content freshness monitoring |
| Timing blindness | INC-2041: outside paging hours | Ensure coverage across all hours |
| Upstream detection | INC-2041: cert expiry unknown | Monitor upstream service dependencies |

An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

Based on the incidents we've reviewed, our monitoring has exposed several critical gaps:

## 1. **Complete Blind Spots During Infrastructure Events**

**INC-2093 - Registry Outage (42 minutes)** [D11:0]
- **Gap**: Monitoring relied entirely on the registry for the agent list, so when the registry was unreachable, the overview dashboard went completely blank
- **Impact**: On-call engineer had zero visibility into which agents were affected during the outage
- **Root cause**: The monitoring lost sight of every agent; its agent list comes from the registry and there was no alert on the standby falling 38 minutes behind

## 2. **Stale-Correct Behavior Without Detection**

**INC-2067 - Research Agent Serving Outdated Results** [D10:0]
- **Gap**: No automated alert fired because the agent itself functioned correctly (no errors occurred)
- **Impact**: User discovered four days later that answers contained policies changed just before they were cached
- **Root cause**: kb-search cache TTL was misconfigured from 7 hours to 7 days

## 3. **Timing-Based Alert Blindness**

**INC-2041 - Billing Agent Invoicing Failures** [D09:0]
- **Gap**: Error rate alert fired but it was "outside paging hours" so nobody saw it immediately
- **Impact**: 1,140 invoices went out late before on-call engineer arrived
- **Root cause**: Payments-gateway timeouts from expiring certificates were treated as transient and retried repeatedly

## 4. **Upstream Failure Detection Gap**

In INC-2041, monitoring could only detect downstream timeouts, not the root cause:
- Auth-service intermediate certificate had expired at 06:00
- Payments-gateway checked and failed, then timed out instead of returning an error
- Monitoring never alerted to certificate expiration or auth-service health

|----------|---------|-----------------|
| Lost agent visibility | INC-2093: blank dashboard | Keep last good agent list when registry unreachable |
| Missing lag alerts | INC-2093: 38-min catch-up gap | Fire alert when standby >60s behind |
| Silent staleness | INC-2067: no alerts at all | Need content freshness monitoring |
| Timing blindness | INC-2041: outside paging hours | Ensure coverage across all hours |
| Upstream detection | INC-2041: cert expiry unknown | Monitor upstream service dependencies |

answers:
Based on my search of incident documentation, here are the key monitoring gaps that our major incidents have exposed:

## **INC-2093: Registry Outage During Database Failover (42 minutes)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **No agent visibility during registry downtime**: Monitoring showed "no agents at all" when the registry was unreachable, making it impossible to determine which services were affected [D11:2]
- **No standby lag detection**: The standby database fell 38 minutes behind the primary with no alerts firing. Failover should have taken ~5 minutes but took 42 because nothing alerted on that lag [D11:2]
- **Blank dashboard during outages**: While `RegistryUnreachable` alert fired and paged the on-call engineer, the overview dashboard went blank instead of showing meaningful status [D11:1]

**What We Changed:** An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind; monitoring keeps the last good agent list when the registry is unreachable; `support_agent` tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently [D11:3]

---

## **INC-2067: Research Agent Returning Outdated Results (1 week)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **No freshness/accuracy monitoring**: Latency and error rate looked "better than usual" since cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measured whether results were current [D10:2]
- **Silent degradation**: The agent operated normally while returning stale content from KB articles with incorrect TTL settings [D10:1]

**What We Changed**: KB-search cache settings now require approval if TTL exceeds 24 hours; each kb-search result carries article update dates that agents include in citations [D10:3]

---

## **INC-2041: Billing Agent Unable to Issue Invoices (2h 15min)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **Alerting outside business hours**: `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired but didn't page because it occurred outside paging hours [D09:1]
- **Timeout masking root cause**: Retries masked the underlying certificate timeout issue until the step limit ran out [D09:2]

---

### **Summary of Core Gaps:**
1. **Service dependency monitoring**: No alerts on downstream service health or replication lag
2. **Quality-of-service metrics**: No measurement of answer/content freshness beyond latency/error rates
3. **Business-hours aligned alerting**: Critical issues can occur during off-hours without immediate notification
4. **Aggregated visibility**: During registry failures, no fallback mechanism preserved agent inventory visibility

## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. ## Failover

Many failover systems use just two systems, the primary and the standby, connected by some kind of heartbeat mechanism to continually verify the connectivity between the two and the viability of the primary. It is also possible to use a third system (called a witness server) to prevent some cases of inappropriate failover, but the additional complexity might not be worthwhile unless it is set up with sufficient care and rigorous testing.

PostgreSQL does not provide the system software required to identify a failure on the primary and notify the standby database server. Many such tools exist and are well integrated with the operating system facilities required for successful failover, such as IP address migration.

### User's Overview

During hot standby, the parameter `transaction_read_only` is always true and may not be changed. But as long as no attempt is made to modify the database, connections during hot standby will act much like any other database connection. If failover or switchover occurs, the database will switch to normal processing mode. Sessions will remain connected while the server changes mode. Once hot standby finishes, it will be possible to initiate read-write transactions (even from a session begun during hot standby).
</source>

To trigger failover of a log-shipping standby server, run `pg_ctl promote` or call `pg_promote()`. If you're setting up reporting servers that are only used to offload read-only queries from the primary, not for high availability purposes, you don't need to promote.

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:82" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Failover" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">

If the primary server fails then the standby server should begin failover procedures.

If the standby server fails then no failover need take place. <source id="D13:2" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Why the cap exists" date="2026-09-01" type="official">
## Why the cap exists

In March, a loop bug made `billing_agent` retry failed invoices without a step limit, and it used $2,900 of model calls in one night. The cap limits what any single bug can cost. It isn't a budget target: normal usage is about $2,200 a month.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D13:1" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Raising the limit" date="2026-09-01" type="official">
## Raising the limit

Send a request to the Finance operations lead with the new cap, the reason, and the expected monthly volume of invoices. Raises up to $6,000 are approved by the Finance operations lead. Above that, the CFO approves.
</source>

Based on my search of incident documentation, here are the key monitoring gaps that our major incidents have exposed:

## **INC-2093: Registry Outage During Database Failover (42 minutes)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **No agent visibility during registry downtime**: Monitoring showed "no agents at all" when the registry was unreachable, making it impossible to determine which services were affected [D11:2]
- **No standby lag detection**: The standby database fell 38 minutes behind the primary with no alerts firing. Failover should have taken ~5 minutes but took 42 because nothing alerted on that lag [D11:2]
- **Blank dashboard during outages**: While `RegistryUnreachable` alert fired and paged the on-call engineer, the overview dashboard went blank instead of showing meaningful status [D11:1]

**What We Changed:** An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind; monitoring keeps the last good agent list when the registry is unreachable; `support_agent` tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently [D11:3]

---

## **INC-2067: Research Agent Returning Outdated Results (1 week)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **No freshness/accuracy monitoring**: Latency and error rate looked "better than usual" since cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measured whether results were current [D10:2]
- **Silent degradation**: The agent operated normally while returning stale content from KB articles with incorrect TTL settings [D10:1]

**What We Changed**: KB-search cache settings now require approval if TTL exceeds 24 hours; each kb-search result carries article update dates that agents include in citations [D10:3]

---

## **INC-2041: Billing Agent Unable to Issue Invoices (2h 15min)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **Alerting outside business hours**: `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired but didn't page because it occurred outside paging hours [D09:1]
- **Timeout masking root cause**: Retries masked the underlying certificate timeout issue until the step limit ran out [D09:2]

---

### **Summary of Core Gaps:**
1. **Service dependency monitoring**: No alerts on downstream service health or replication lag
2. **Quality-of-service metrics**: No measurement of answer/content freshness beyond latency/error rates
3. **Business-hours aligned alerting**: Critical issues can occur during off-hours without immediate notification
4. **Aggregated visibility**: During registry failures, no fallback mechanism preserved agent inventory visibility

<source id="D13:2" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Why the cap exists" date="2026-09-01" type="official">
## Why the cap exists

In March, a loop bug made `billing_agent` retry failed invoices without a step limit, and it used $2,900 of model calls in one night. The cap limits what any single bug can cost. It isn't a budget target: normal usage is about $2,200 a month.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D13:1" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Raising the limit" date="2026-09-01" type="official">
## Raising the limit

Send a request to the Finance operations lead with the new cap, the reason, and the expected monthly volume of invoices. Raises up to $6,000 are approved by the Finance operations lead. Above that, the CFO approves.
</source>

Based on my search of incident documentation, here are the key monitoring gaps that our major incidents have exposed:

## **INC-2093: Registry Outage During Database Failover (42 minutes)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **No agent visibility during registry downtime**: Monitoring showed "no agents at all" when the registry was unreachable, making it impossible to determine which services were affected [D11:2]
- **No standby lag detection**: The standby database fell 38 minutes behind the primary with no alerts firing. Failover should have taken ~5 minutes but took 42 because nothing alerted on that lag [D11:2]
- **Blank dashboard during outages**: While `RegistryUnreachable` alert fired and paged the on-call engineer, the overview dashboard went blank instead of showing meaningful status [D11:1]

**What We Changed:** An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind; monitoring keeps the last good agent list when the registry is unreachable; `support_agent` tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently [D11:3]

---

## **INC-2067: Research Agent Returning Outdated Results (1 week)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **No freshness/accuracy monitoring**: Latency and error rate looked "better than usual" since cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measured whether results were current [D10:2]
- **Silent degradation**: The agent operated normally while returning stale content from KB articles with incorrect TTL settings [D10:1]

**What We Changed**: KB-search cache settings now require approval if TTL exceeds 24 hours; each kb-search result carries article update dates that agents include in citations [D10:3]

---

## **INC-2041: Billing Agent Unable to Issue Invoices (2h 15min)**

**Gaps Exposed:**
- **Alerting outside business hours**: `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired but didn't page because it occurred outside paging hours [D09:1]
- **Timeout masking root cause**: Retries masked the underlying certificate timeout issue until the step limit ran out [D09:2]

---

### **Summary of Core Gaps:**
1. **Service dependency monitoring**: No alerts on downstream service health or replication lag
2. **Quality-of-service metrics**: No measurement of answer/content freshness beyond latency/error rates
3. **Business-hours aligned alerting**: Critical issues can occur during off-hours without immediate notification
4. **Aggregated visibility**: During registry failures, no fallback mechanism preserved agent inventory visibility

answers:
Based on the incident documentation, here are the key monitoring gaps that our incidents have exposed:

## 1. **No Measurement of Result Freshness**
During INC-2067 (research_agent returning outdated results), the agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual because cached answers were fast and never failed. Nothing in monitoring measured whether results were actually current—only a person manually comparing answers against sources detected the problem after a week [D10:2].

## 2. **Missing Standby Lag Detection**
In INC-2093 (registry outage during database failover), the failover took 42 minutes because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary. There was nothing alerting on that initial lag—the failover should have taken ~5 minutes but didn't [D11:2].

## 3. **Complete Loss of Visibility When Registry Is Unreachable**
When the registry went down in INC-2093, monitoring lost sight of every single agent for the entire outage period. The dashboard went blank instead of showing degraded performance, leaving on-call engineers unable to identify which agents were affected [D11:0][D11:2].

## 4. **Silent Failures**
- `support_agent` would fail silently when the registry was unavailable rather than informing users of registry unavailability [D11:3]
- In INC-2041, the billing agent treated certificate-checking timeouts as transient errors and kept retrying until its step limit ran out before flagging a real problem [D09:2]

## 5. **Rate Limiting Masquerading as Latency**
Agents being rate-limited return `REG-1009` errors with `Retry-After` headers, but these appear as latency spikes since requests wait before succeeding. Monitoring captures only p50/p95 response times without diagnosing whether high latency is due to rate limiting [D05:4][D01:8].

## 6. **Timeout Accumulation Not Caught Early**
The billing_agent didn't surface its problems until certificates expired and hundreds of timeouts accumulated across its retries—there was no threshold alerting for multiple consecutive failures from the same service [D09:2].

---

**Summary**: We monitor response time, error rate, and session count, but not result freshness, latency root causes (like rate limiting), or silent failures. Our agent list refreshes every 30 seconds from the registry, so when the registry fails, we lose visibility entirely.

</source>

content.text:
Based on the incident documentation, here are the key monitoring gaps that our incidents have exposed:

## 1. **No Measurement of Result Freshness**
During INC-2067 (research_agent returning outdated results), the agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual because cached answers were fast and never failed. Nothing in monitoring measured whether results were actually current—only a person manually comparing answers against sources detected the problem after a week [D10:2].

## 2. **Missing Standby Lag Detection**
In INC-2093 (registry outage during database failover), the failover took 42 minutes because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary. There was nothing alerting on that initial lag—the failover should have taken ~5 minutes but didn't [D11:2].

## 3. **Complete Loss of Visibility When Registry Is Unreachable**
When the registry went down in INC-2093, monitoring lost sight of every single agent for the entire outage period. The dashboard went blank instead of showing degraded performance, leaving on-call engineers unable to identify which agents were affected [D11:0][D11:2].

## 4. **Silent Failures**
- `support_agent` would fail silently when the registry was unavailable rather than informing users of registry unavailability [D11:3]
- In INC-2041, the billing agent treated certificate-checking timeouts as transient errors and kept retrying until its step limit ran out before flagging a real problem [D09:2]

## 5. **Rate Limiting Masquerading as Latency**
Agents being rate-limited return `REG-1009` errors with `Retry-After` headers, but these appear as latency spikes since requests wait before succeeding. Monitoring captures only p50/p95 response times without diagnosing whether high latency is due to rate limiting [D05:4][D01:8].

## 6. **Timeout Accumulation Not Caught Early**
The billing_agent didn't surface its problems until certificates expired and hundreds of timeouts accumulated across its retries—there was no threshold alerting for multiple consecutive failures from the same service [D09:2].

---

**Summary**: We monitor response time, error rate, and session count, but not result freshness, latency root causes (like rate limiting), or silent failures. Our agent list refreshes every 30 seconds from the registry, so when the registry fails, we lose visibility entirely.

Nothing in monitoring measured whether results were actually current—only a person manually comparing answers against sources detected the problem after a week [D10:2].

## 2. **Missing Standby Lag Detection**
In INC-2093 (registry outage during database failover), the failover took 42 minutes because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary. There was nothing alerting on that initial lag—the failover should have taken ~5 minutes but didn't [D11:2].

## 3. **Complete Loss of Visibility When Registry Is Unreachable**
When the registry went down in INC-2093, monitoring lost sight of every single agent for the entire outage period. The dashboard went blank instead of showing degraded performance, leaving on-call engineers unable to identify which agents were affected [D11:0][D11:2].

## 4. **Silent Failures**
- `support_agent` would fail silently when the registry was unavailable rather than informing users of registry unavailability [D11:3]
- In INC-2041, the billing agent treated certificate-checking timeouts as transient errors and kept retrying until its step limit ran out before flagging a real problem [D09:2]

## 5. **Rate Limiting Masquerading as Latency**
Agents being rate-limited return `REG-1009` errors with `Retry-After` headers, but these appear as latency spikes since requests wait before succeeding. Monitoring captures only p50/p95 response times without diagnosing whether high latency is due to rate limiting [D05:4][D01:8].

## 6. **Timeout Accumulation Not Caught Early**
The billing_agent didn't surface its problems until certificates expired and hundreds of timeouts accumulated across its retries—there was no threshold alerting for multiple consecutive failures from the same service [D09:2].

---

**Summary**: We monitor response time, error rate, and session count, but not result freshness, latency root causes (like rate limiting), or silent failures. Our agent list refreshes every 30 seconds from the registry, so when the registry fails, we lose visibility entirely.

### Administrator's Overview

Advisory locks work normally in recovery, including deadlock detection. Note that advisory locks are never WAL logged, so it is impossible for an advisory lock on either the primary or the standby to conflict with WAL replay. Nor is it possible to acquire an advisory lock on the primary and have it initiate a similar advisory lock on the standby. Advisory locks relate only to the server on which they are acquired.

## External labels and remote read

The `external_labels` setting in `global` affects remote read on both sides:

- **Exposing remote read:** Prometheus appends `external_labels` to every time series returned via `/api/v1/read`. The labels are not stored in TSDB; they are added at response time. Incoming equality matchers that match an external label are rewritten to match the empty string so that TSDB can satisfy the query.
- **Using remote read:** The querying Prometheus sends its own `external_labels` as additional equality matchers in the request, then strips them from the response.
</source>

Alerting rules are configured in Prometheus in the same way as recording
rules.

groups:

  labels:

  rules:
  - alert: HighRequestLatency

    labels:

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:6" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Deleting an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Deleting an agent

`DELETE /agents/{agent_id}` removes an agent's record permanently. Prefer setting `status` to `retired`, which keeps the record and its change history. Delete only agents that were created by mistake.
</source>

The `annotations` clause specifies a set of informational labels that can be used to store longer additional information such as alert descriptions or runbook links. The annotation values can be templated.

   // Merge logic: last-write-wins based on UpdatedAt timestamp

5. **Lack of Proactive Alerts for Infrastructure Events**: INC-2093 occurred "during database failover" - suggesting infrastructure events aren't being proactively monitored at the right granularity.


6. **Response Latency Potential**: Prolonged incident durations hint at possible delays in detection or alert routing mechanisms.

The following binary histogram trim operators exist in Prometheus:

* `</` (trim upper): removes all observations above a threshold value
* `>/` (trim lower): removes all observations below a threshold value

Histogram trim operators are defined between vector/scalar and vector/vector value pairs,
where the left hand side is a native histogram (either exponential or NHCB),
and the right hand side is a float threshold value.
</source>

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.

## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md:7" doc="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md" title="Overview" section="Overview > When does it fit?" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## When does it fit?

Prometheus works well for recording any purely numeric time series. It fits
both machine-centric monitoring as well as monitoring of highly dynamic
service-oriented architectures. In a world of microservices, its support for
multi-dimensional data collection and querying is a particular strength.

Prometheus is designed for reliability, to be the system you go to
during an outage to allow you to quickly diagnose problems. Each Prometheus
server is standalone, not depending on network storage or other remote services.
You can rely on it when other parts of your infrastructure are broken, and
you do not need to set up extensive infrastructure to use it.
</source>

### Administrator's Overview

Advisory locks work normally in recovery, including deadlock detection. Note that advisory locks are never WAL logged, so it is impossible for an advisory lock on either the primary or the standby to conflict with WAL replay. Nor is it possible to acquire an advisory lock on the primary and have it initiate a similar advisory lock on the standby. Advisory locks relate only to the server on which they are acquired.

## External labels and remote read

The `external_labels` setting in `global` affects remote read on both sides:

- **Exposing remote read:** Prometheus appends `external_labels` to every time series returned via `/api/v1/read`. The labels are not stored in TSDB; they are added at response time. Incoming equality matchers that match an external label are rewritten to match the empty string so that TSDB can satisfy the query.
- **Using remote read:** The querying Prometheus sends its own `external_labels` as additional equality matchers in the request, then strips them from the response.
</source>

Alerting rules are configured in Prometheus in the same way as recording
rules.

An example rules file with an alert would be:

```yaml
groups:
- name: example
  labels:
    team: myteam
  rules:
  - alert: HighRequestLatency
    expr: job:request_latency_seconds:mean5m{job="myjob"} > 0.5
    for: 10m
    keep_firing_for: 5m
    labels:

## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

### Silence Creation and Updates

When a silence is created or updated on any instance:

   }

### Histogram trim operators

The following binary histogram trim operators exist in Prometheus:

* `</` (trim upper): removes all observations above a threshold value
* `>/` (trim lower): removes all observations below a threshold value

Histogram trim operators are defined between vector/scalar and vector/vector value pairs,
where the left hand side is a native histogram (either exponential or NHCB),
and the right hand side is a float threshold value.
</source>

## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md:7" doc="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md" title="Overview" section="Overview > When does it fit?" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## When does it fit?

Prometheus works well for recording any purely numeric time series. It fits
both machine-centric monitoring as well as monitoring of highly dynamic
service-oriented architectures. In a world of microservices, its support for
multi-dimensional data collection and querying is a particular strength.

Prometheus is designed for reliability, to be the system you go to
during an outage to allow you to quickly diagnose problems. Each Prometheus
server is standalone, not depending on network storage or other remote services.
You can rely on it when other parts of your infrastructure are broken, and
you do not need to set up extensive infrastructure to use it.
</source>

## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. - Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

answers:
Based on my analysis of our incident history, here are the key monitoring gaps that incidents have exposed:

## 1. **No Freshness/Result Currency Monitoring** (INC-2067)
- Monitoring only tracks latency and error rates, not whether results are current
- The kb-search cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days without triggering any alerts
- Only discovered when a user compared an answer with the source
- Took **10,080 minutes (1 full week)** to notice this issue

## 2. **No Failover Lag Detection** (INC-2093)
- During the registry-db failover, nothing alerted when the standby fell **38 minutes behind** the primary
- Expected failover time was ~5 minutes, but it took 42 minutes total
- No alert fired when the standby was falling too far behind

## 3. **Blind Spot During Service Outages** (INC-2093)
- When registry-api was unavailable, monitoring showed **no agents at all**
- On-call engineer couldn't tell which specific agents were affected
- Monitoring loses sight of every agent when registry is unreachable

## 4. **Poor Dependency Chain Visibility** (INC-2041, INC-2093)
- It wasn't immediately obvious how auth-service failures cascade to billing_agent
- The dependency chain between auth-service → registry → various agents wasn't clearly monitored
- Multiple services failing silently made root cause identification difficult

## 5. **Config Change Detection Gaps**
- Agent config changes (like cache TTL settings) didn't trigger monitoring alerts
- Critical configuration changes were treated like code review without special oversight
- kb-search's cache settings weren't reviewed with appropriate approval gates

## 6. **Support Flow Failure Silences**
- `support_agent` would fail silently when registry was unavailable instead of providing clear feedback
- This masked the underlying infrastructure issue to users

---

**Improvements already made:**
- Alerts now fire when standby falls more than 60 seconds behind [D11:3]
- Monitoring keeps last good agent list when registry is unreachable [D11:3]
- `support_agent` now tells users registry is unavailable [D11:3]
- kb-search cache settings now need Search team approval with 24+ hour TTL [D10:3]
- Auth-service alerts 30 days before certificate expiration [D09:3]

The core pattern across incidents: we monitor individual components well, but the systems-level dependencies and change impacts often fall through the cracks.

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

Based on my analysis of our incident history, here are the key monitoring gaps that incidents have exposed:

## 1. **No Freshness/Result Currency Monitoring** (INC-2067)
- Monitoring only tracks latency and error rates, not whether results are current
- The kb-search cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days without triggering any alerts
- Only discovered when a user compared an answer with the source
- Took **10,080 minutes (1 full week)** to notice this issue

## 2. **No Failover Lag Detection** (INC-2093)
- During the registry-db failover, nothing alerted when the standby fell **38 minutes behind** the primary
- Expected failover time was ~5 minutes, but it took 42 minutes total
- No alert fired when the standby was falling too far behind

## 3. **Blind Spot During Service Outages** (INC-2093)
- When registry-api was unavailable, monitoring showed **no agents at all**
- On-call engineer couldn't tell which specific agents were affected
- Monitoring loses sight of every agent when registry is unreachable

## 4. **Poor Dependency Chain Visibility** (INC-2041, INC-2093)
- It wasn't immediately obvious how auth-service failures cascade to billing_agent
- The dependency chain between auth-service → registry → various agents wasn't clearly monitored
- Multiple services failing silently made root cause identification difficult

## 5. **Config Change Detection Gaps**
- Agent config changes (like cache TTL settings) didn't trigger monitoring alerts
- Critical configuration changes were treated like code review without special oversight
- kb-search's cache settings weren't reviewed with appropriate approval gates

## 6. **Support Flow Failure Silences**
- `support_agent` would fail silently when registry was unavailable instead of providing clear feedback
- This masked the underlying infrastructure issue to users

---

**Improvements already made:**
- Alerts now fire when standby falls more than 60 seconds behind [D11:3]
- Monitoring keeps last good agent list when registry is unreachable [D11:3]
- `support_agent` now tells users registry is unavailable [D11:3]
- kb-search cache settings now need Search team approval with 24+ hour TTL [D10:3]
- Auth-service alerts 30 days before certificate expiration [D09:3]

The core pattern across incidents: we monitor individual components well, but the systems-level dependencies and change impacts often fall through the cracks.

## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.

Based on my analysis of our incident history, here are the key monitoring gaps that incidents have exposed:

## 1. **No Freshness/Result Currency Monitoring** (INC-2067)
- Monitoring only tracks latency and error rates, not whether results are current
- The kb-search cache TTL was changed from 7 hours to 7 days without triggering any alerts
- Only discovered when a user compared an answer with the source
- Took **10,080 minutes (1 full week)** to notice this issue

## 2. **No Failover Lag Detection** (INC-2093)
- During the registry-db failover, nothing alerted when the standby fell **38 minutes behind** the primary
- Expected failover time was ~5 minutes, but it took 42 minutes total
- No alert fired when the standby was falling too far behind

## 3. **Blind Spot During Service Outages** (INC-2093)
- When registry-api was unavailable, monitoring showed **no agents at all**
- On-call engineer couldn't tell which specific agents were affected
- Monitoring loses sight of every agent when registry is unreachable

## 4. **Poor Dependency Chain Visibility** (INC-2041, INC-2093)
- It wasn't immediately obvious how auth-service failures cascade to billing_agent
- The dependency chain between auth-service → registry → various agents wasn't clearly monitored
- Multiple services failing silently made root cause identification difficult

## 5. **Config Change Detection Gaps**
- Agent config changes (like cache TTL settings) didn't trigger monitoring alerts
- Critical configuration changes were treated like code review without special oversight
- kb-search's cache settings weren't reviewed with appropriate approval gates

## 6. **Support Flow Failure Silences**
- `support_agent` would fail silently when registry was unavailable instead of providing clear feedback
- This masked the underlying infrastructure issue to users

---

**Improvements already made:**
- Alerts now fire when standby falls more than 60 seconds behind [D11:3]
- Monitoring keeps last good agent list when registry is unreachable [D11:3]
- `support_agent` now tells users registry is unavailable [D11:3]
- kb-search cache settings now need Search team approval with 24+ hour TTL [D10:3]
- Auth-service alerts 30 days before certificate expiration [D09:3]

The core pattern across incidents: we monitor individual components well, but the systems-level dependencies and change impacts often fall through the cracks.

content.content:
<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D03:2" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.4 — 2026-05-12" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.4 — 2026-05-12

- Lowered the rate limit from 100 to 60 requests per minute per key. Some internal dashboards were polling hard enough to slow the registry for agents.
- Rate-limited responses (`REG-1009`) now include a `Retry-After` header.
</source>

<source id="D08:4" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Polling the registry from your own dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D03:4" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.2 — 2026-01-20" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.2 — 2026-01-20

- `GET /agents` now pages with `cursor` and `next_cursor`. The `offset` parameter still works but is deprecated.
- Page size is set with `limit`: default 20, maximum 100.
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="D08:4" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Polling the registry from your own dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D03:2" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.4 — 2026-05-12" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.4 — 2026-05-12

- Lowered the rate limit from 100 to 60 requests per minute per key. Some internal dashboards were polling hard enough to slow the registry for agents.
- Rate-limited responses (`REG-1009`) now include a `Retry-After` header.
</source>

<source id="D08:3" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Dashboards

Each agent has a panel with latency, error rate and sessions. The overview dashboard shows every active agent on one screen, sorted by p95. Panels refresh every 30 seconds and lag real time by up to a minute.
</source>

<source id="D08:2" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > When RegistryUnreachable fires" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## When RegistryUnreachable fires

Check the registry's status page first. While the registry is down, monitoring can't refresh its agent list, so dashboards may show no agents at all even though the agents are still running. Don't read an empty dashboard as "every agent is down."
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/examples.md:8" doc="prometheus-server/querying/examples.md" title="Query examples" section="Query examples > Using functions, operators, etc." date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Using functions, operators, etc.

As another case for measuring _amount of time_, for example a boolean metric
representing a service level agreement (SLA) being met divided by the total
time, will give the SLA ratio:

    integral(service_sla_ok[7d]) / (3600 * 24 * 7)
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/getting_started.md:7" doc="prometheus-server/getting_started.md" title="Getting started" section="Getting started > Using the expression browser" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Using the expression browser

This should return a number of different time series (along with the latest value
recorded for each), each with the metric name
`prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds`, but with different labels. These
labels designate different latency percentiles and target group intervals.

If we are interested only in 99th percentile latencies, we could use this
query:

```
prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds{quantile="0.99"}
```

To count the number of returned time series, you could write:

```
count(prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds)
```

For more about the expression language, see the
expression language documentation.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:41" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `histogram_quantiles()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `histogram_quantiles()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤
φ ≤ 1) from a classic
histogram or from
a native histogram. Quantile calculation works the same way as in `histogram_quantile()`.
The second argument (a string) specifies the label name that is used to identify different quantiles in the query result.
```
histogram_quantiles(sum(rate(foo[1m])), "quantile", 0.9, 0.99)
# => {quantile="0.9"} 123
     {quantile="0.99"} 128
```

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. ## Using the expression browser

This should return a number of different time series (along with the latest value
recorded for each), each with the metric name

prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds{quantile="0.99"}

To count the number of returned time series, you could write:

count(prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds)

## `histogram_quantiles()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤
φ ≤ 1) from a classic
histogram or from
a native histogram. Quantile calculation works the same way as in `histogram_quantile()`.
The second argument (a string) specifies the label name that is used to identify different quantiles in the query result.
```
histogram_quantiles(sum(rate(foo[1m])), "quantile", 0.9, 0.99)
# => {quantile="0.9"} 123
     {quantile="0.99"} 128
```
</source>

### Histogram trim operators

The following binary histogram trim operators exist in Prometheus:

* `</` (trim upper): removes all observations above a threshold value
* `>/` (trim lower): removes all observations below a threshold value

Histogram trim operators are defined between vector/scalar and vector/vector value pairs,
where the left hand side is a native histogram (either exponential or NHCB),
and the right hand side is a float threshold value.
</source>

## `histogram_quantiles()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤
φ ≤ 1) from a classic
histogram or from
a native histogram. Quantile calculation works the same way as in `histogram_quantile()`.
The second argument (a string) specifies the label name that is used to identify different quantiles in the query result.
```
histogram_quantiles(sum(rate(foo[1m])), "quantile", 0.9, 0.99)
# => {quantile="0.9"} 123
     {quantile="0.99"} 128
```
</source>

### Summary

**Rule:** In OM 2.0, a Summary Sample must contain Count, Sum, and a set of quantiles. In OM 1.0 these were all may. Exposers that previously omitted count or sum must now include them.

OM 1.0:
```
# TYPE http_request_duration_seconds_summary summary
http_request_duration_seconds_summary{quantile="0.5"} 0.013
http_request_duration_seconds_summary{quantile="0.9"} 0.025
http_request_duration_seconds_summary{quantile="0.99"} 0.10
http_request_duration_seconds_summary_sum 172.5
http_request_duration_seconds_summary_count 1027

```
# TYPE http_request_duration_seconds_summary summary
http_request_duration_seconds_summary {count:1027,sum:172.5,quantile:[0.5:0.013,0.9:0.025,0.99:0.10]}
```

## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

The following binary histogram trim operators exist in Prometheus:

* `>/` (trim lower): removes all observations below a threshold value

### Histogram trim operators

In case the threshold value is not aligned to one of the bucket boundaries of the histogram,
either linear (for NHCB and zero buckets of exponential histogram) or exponential (for non zero
bucket of exponential histogram) interpolation is applied to compute the estimated count

</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.

An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

The following binary histogram trim operators exist in Prometheus:

* `>/` (trim lower): removes all observations below a threshold value

## `histogram_quantiles()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤
φ ≤ 1) from a classic
histogram or from
a native histogram. Quantile calculation works the same way as in `histogram_quantile()`.
The second argument (a string) specifies the label name that is used to identify different quantiles in the query result.

## Reliability

When the operating system sends a write request to the storage hardware, there is little it can do to make sure the data has arrived at a truly non-volatile storage area. Rather, it is the administrator's responsibility to make certain that all storage components ensure integrity for both data and file-system metadata. Avoid disk controllers that have non-battery-backed write caches. At the drive level, disable write-back caching if the drive cannot guarantee the data will be written before shutdown. #### Planning for High Availability

If primary restarts while commits are waiting for acknowledgment, those waiting transactions will be marked fully committed once the primary database recovers. There is no way to be certain that all standbys have received all outstanding WAL data at time of the crash of the primary. Some transactions may not show as committed on the standby, even though they show as committed on the primary. The guarantee we offer is that the application will not receive explicit acknowledgment of the successful commit of a transaction until the WAL data is known to be safely received by all the synchronous standbys.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

- Added the `tier` field to every agent. Existing agents were set to `standard`.
- Each tier now has an allowlist of models. Assigning a model outside it returns `REG-1007`.

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1005` | `AGENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No agent has this `agent_id`. Ids are case-sensitive. |
| `REG-1006` | `AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` | 409 | An agent with this `agent_id` already exists, including a retired one. |
| `REG-1007` | `MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED` | 422 | The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model. |
| `REG-1008` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | The body is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type. The message names the field. |
| `REG-1010` | `MODEL_DEPRECATED` | 422 | The model is deprecated and can't be newly assigned. Currently applies to `claude-legacy`. |

prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds{quantile="0.99"}

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed
