- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

#### Planning for High Availability

If primary restarts while commits are waiting for acknowledgment, those waiting transactions will be marked fully committed once the primary database recovers. There is no way to be certain that all standbys have received all outstanding WAL data at time of the crash of the primary. Some transactions may not show as committed on the standby, even though they show as committed on the primary. The guarantee we offer is that the application will not receive explicit acknowledgment of the successful commit of a transaction until the WAL data is known to be safely received by all the synchronous standbys.
</source>

## Reliability

When the operating system sends a write request to the storage hardware, there is little it can do to make sure the data has arrived at a truly non-volatile storage area. Rather, it is the administrator's responsibility to make certain that all storage components ensure integrity for both data and file-system metadata. Avoid disk controllers that have non-battery-backed write caches. At the drive level, disable write-back caching if the drive cannot guarantee the data will be written before shutdown. If you use SSDs, be aware that many of these do not honor cache flush commands by default. You can test for reliable I/O subsystem behavior using `diskchecker.pl`.
</source>

#### Planning for High Availability

If primary restarts while commits are waiting for acknowledgment, those waiting transactions will be marked fully committed once the primary database recovers. There is no way to be certain that all standbys have received all outstanding WAL data at time of the crash of the primary. Some transactions may not show as committed on the standby, even though they show as committed on the primary. The guarantee we offer is that the application will not receive explicit acknowledgment of the successful commit of a transaction until the WAL data is known to be safely received by all the synchronous standbys.
</source>

## Reliability

When the operating system sends a write request to the storage hardware, there is little it can do to make sure the data has arrived at a truly non-volatile storage area. Rather, it is the administrator's responsibility to make certain that all storage components ensure integrity for both data and file-system metadata. Avoid disk controllers that have non-battery-backed write caches. At the drive level, disable write-back caching if the drive cannot guarantee the data will be written before shutdown. If you use SSDs, be aware that many of these do not honor cache flush commands by default. You can test for reliable I/O subsystem behavior using `diskchecker.pl`.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

## Alertmanager

Any user with access to the Alertmanager HTTP endpoint has access to its data.
They can create and resolve alerts. They can create, modify and delete
silences.

Operators who do not configure any form of authentication must exercise
caution: Alertmanager serves `/api/v2` with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.

the service.

## Pushgateway

Any user with access to the Pushgateway HTTP endpoint can create, modify and
delete the metrics contained within. As the Pushgateway is usually scraped with
`honor_labels` enabled, this means anyone with access to the Pushgateway can
create any time series in Prometheus.

The `--web.enable-admin-api` flag controls access to the
administrative HTTP API, which includes functionality such as wiping all the existing
metric groups. This is disabled by default. If enabled, administrative
functionality will be accessible under the `/api/*/admin/` paths.
</source>

### Overview

If a user wants to create blocks into the TSDB from data that is in
OpenMetrics format, they can do so using backfilling.
However, they should be careful and note that it is not safe to backfill data
from the last 3 hours (the current head block) as this time range may overlap
with the current head block Prometheus is still mutating. Backfilling will
create new TSDB blocks, each containing two hours of metrics data. This limits
the memory requirements of block creation. Compacting the two hour blocks into
larger blocks is later done by the Prometheus server itself.
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D03:3" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.3 — 2026-03-10" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.3 — 2026-03-10

- Added the `tier` field to every agent. Existing agents were set to `standard`.
- Each tier now has an allowlist of models. Assigning a model outside it returns `REG-1007`.
</source>

Based on my search of the company's internal documentation, there is **no information about how to create a new tier** in the available documentation. 

The Registry API documentation does mention:

- Tiers are a property assigned to each agent when they're created (the `tier` field was added in v2.3) [D03:3]
- Each tier has a fixed allowlist of allowed models (e.g., `standard` allows `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`) [D01:7]
- When assigning an agent to a tier, you must specify which tier to use in the `POST /agents` request [D01:4]

However, the documentation only describes tiers as predefined categories (`standard`, `priority`, etc.) with their own model allowlists. There's no guidance on:
- How tiers are created/provisioned
- What permissions or roles are needed to create a new tier
- Any API endpoint for tier management

It appears that tier creation may be handled through a separate administrative process, infrastructure component, or configuration system outside of the public Registry API shown in the documentation. If you need to add a new tier, you should check with your platform team or search the runbooks/administration sections for tier provisioning procedures.

<source id="prometheus-server/storage.md:18" doc="prometheus-server/storage.md" title="Storage" section="Storage > Backfilling from OpenMetrics format > Overview" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### Overview

If a user wants to create blocks into the TSDB from data that is in
OpenMetrics format, they can do so using backfilling.
However, they should be careful and note that it is not safe to backfill data
from the last 3 hours (the current head block) as this time range may overlap
with the current head block Prometheus is still mutating. Backfilling will
create new TSDB blocks, each containing two hours of metrics data. This limits
the memory requirements of block creation. Compacting the two hour blocks into
larger blocks is later done by the Prometheus server itself.
</source>

## Alternative strategies

If an inbound firewall or NAT is preventing you from pulling metrics from
targets, consider moving the Prometheus server behind the network barrier as
well. We generally recommend running Prometheus servers on the same network as
the monitored instances.  Otherwise, consider PushProx,
which allows Prometheus to traverse a firewall or NAT.

For batch jobs that are related to a machine (such as automatic
security update cronjobs or configuration management client runs), expose the
resulting metrics using the Node Exporter's
textfile collector instead of the Pushgateway.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

## Changing the targets list dynamically

```json
[
  {
    "targets": [
      "localhost:9100"
    ],
    "labels": {
      "job": "node"
    }
  },
  {
    "targets": [
      "localhost:9200"
    ],
    "labels": {
      "job": "node"
    }
  }
]
```

When you save the changes, Prometheus will automatically be notified of the new list of targets. The `up{job="node"}` metric should display two instances with `instance` labels `localhost:9100` and `localhost:9200`.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md:15" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md" title="The Zen of Prometheus" section="The Zen of Prometheus > Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

For more context My Philosophy on Alerting.
</source>

<source id="D08:1" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Alerts" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Alerts

| Alert | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `AgentLatencyHigh` | p95 response time above 8 seconds for 10 minutes |
| `AgentErrorRateHigh` | more than 5% of sessions end in an error over 15 minutes |
| `RegistryUnreachable` | three registry polls in a row fail (`MON-2002`) |

Alerts go to the on-call channel and page the on-call engineer between 08:00 and 20:00. Outside those hours, only `RegistryUnreachable` pages.
</source>

<source id="D01:2" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Listing agents" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Listing agents

`GET /agents` returns agents in pages. Pass `limit` to set the page size (default 20, maximum 100). Each response includes a `next_cursor`; pass it back as `cursor` to get the next page. When `next_cursor` is `null`, there are no more pages.

```bash
curl "https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents?limit=50&cursor=eyJpZCI6IDUwfQ" \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

```json
{
  "agents": [
    {"agent_id": "support_agent", "model": "claude-sonnet", "tier": "standard", "status": "active"}
  ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IDEwMH0"
}
```

You can filter by `status` (`active`, `paused` or `retired`) and by `owner`.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}

## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.

```bash
curl "https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents?limit=50&cursor=eyJpZCI6IDUwfQ" \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

```json
{
  "agents": [
    {"agent_id": "support_agent", "model": "claude-sonnet", "tier": "standard", "status": "active"}
  ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IDEwMH0"
}
```

You can filter by `status` (`active`, `paused` or `retired`) and by `owner`.

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:5" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Comparison of Different Solutions" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:2" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Listing agents" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Listing agents

`GET /agents` returns agents in pages. Pass `limit` to set the page size (default 20, maximum 100). Each response includes a `next_cursor`; pass it back as `cursor` to get the next page. When `next_cursor` is `null`, there are no more pages.

```bash
curl "https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents?limit=50&cursor=eyJpZCI6IDUwfQ" \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

```json
{
  "agents": [
    {"agent_id": "support_agent", "model": "claude-sonnet", "tier": "standard", "status": "active"}
  ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IDEwMH0"
}
```

You can filter by `status` (`active`, `paused` or `retired`) and by `owner`.
</source>

## Registry key errors

If an agent starts getting `REG-1003` after a key rotation, some process is still holding the old key. Usually it's a cron job or a second deployment nobody remembered. <source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

## When to rotate

Rotate an agent's registry key every 90 days, and immediately if the key may have been exposed: written to a log, pasted in a chat, or committed to a repository. An exposed key is rotated first and investigated second.

<source id="D06:3" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 3: Verify" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 3: Verify

From the agent's environment, call `GET /agents/me` with the new key. It should return the agent you rotated. If it returns `REG-1002`, the secret holds a truncated or mistyped key.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

## Registry key errors

If an agent starts getting `REG-1003` after a key rotation, some process is still holding the old key. Usually it's a cron job or a second deployment nobody remembered. <source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.

## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

## Reading one agent

`GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id.

```json
{
  "agent_id": "research_agent",
  "model": "claude-legacy",
  "tier": "standard",
  "owner": "research-team",
  "status": "active",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z"
}
```

`GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect.
</source>

## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

</source>

## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.

## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

## My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?

Check its status first: someone may have paused it, or it may have hit a spending cap. Then check whether it's on a model that's being switched off. If it's running but every task fails, look at the errors in its logs. An error code starting with `REG-` comes from the registry, and the error code reference explains each one.
</source>

<source id="D14:4" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Who do I ask about my agent's costs?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Who do I ask about my agent's costs?

Your team's budget holder for day-to-day questions. Some agents have spending caps managed by Finance; if yours does, Finance will have told you.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D14:0" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## My agent suddenly stopped answering. What happened?

Check its status first: someone may have paused it, or it may have hit a spending cap. Then check whether it's on a model that's being switched off. If it's running but every task fails, look at the errors in its logs. An error code starting with `REG-` comes from the registry, and the error code reference explains each one.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">

|---|---|

</source>

## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

To manually inspect which alerts are active (pending or firing), navigate to

## Delay `__name__` label removal for PromQL engine

`--enable-feature=promql-delayed-name-removal`

When enabled, Prometheus will change the way in which the `__name__` label is removed from PromQL query results (for functions and expressions for which this is necessary). Specifically, it will delay the removal to the last step of the query evaluation, instead of every time an expression or function creating derived metrics is evaluated.

Based on the documentation, you can mute alerts about individual components when the whole cluster is unreachable using **Alertmanager Inhibitions**. Here's how it works:

## Alertmanager Inhibitions [D07:4]

**Inhibition** is a concept of suppressing notifications for certain alerts if certain other alerts are already firing.

### Example Use Case
> **An alert is firing that informs that an entire cluster is not reachable. Alertmanager can be configured to mute all other alerts concerning this cluster if that particular alert is firing.**

This prevents notifications for hundreds or thousands of firing alerts that are unrelated to the actual issue.

### How to Configure

Inhibitions are configured through the **Alertmanager's configuration file**. You'd need to set up rules where:
- A higher-priority alert detects the whole cluster being unreachable
- Other alerts for individual components within that cluster are inhibited (silenced) when that parent alert is firing

---

**Alternative Option**: There are also **Silences** available [D07:5], which mute alerts for a given time and are configured in the Alertmanager web interface. However, silences don't automatically react to specific alerts—they're more manual/time-based.

Would you like help looking up your specific configuration file or any examples of inhibition setup?

## Architecture Overview

An Alertmanager cluster consists of multiple Alertmanager instances that communicate using a gossip protocol. Each instance:

- Receives alerts independently from Prometheus servers
- Participates in a peer-to-peer gossip mesh
- Replicates state (silences and notification log) to other cluster members
- Processes and sends notifications independently

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:1" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Design Goals" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Design Goals

The Alertmanager HA implementation is designed around three core principles:

1. **Single pane view and management** - Silences and alerts can be viewed and managed from any cluster member, providing a unified operational experience
2. **Survive cluster split-brain with "fail open"** - During network partitions, Alertmanager prefers to send duplicate notifications rather than miss critical alerts
3. **At-least-once delivery** - The system guarantees that notifications are delivered at least once, in line with the fail-open philosophy

These goals prioritize operational reliability and alert delivery over strict exactly-once semantics.
</source>

## Sending alert notifications

Prometheus's alerting rules are good at figuring what is broken *right now*, but
they are not a fully-fledged notification solution. Another layer is needed to
add summarization, notification rate limiting, silencing and alert dependencies
on top of the simple alert definitions. In Prometheus's ecosystem, the
Alertmanager takes on this
role. Thus, Prometheus may be configured to periodically send information about
alert states to an Alertmanager instance, which then takes care of dispatching
the right notifications.
Prometheus can be configured to automatically discover available
Alertmanager instances through its service discovery integrations.
</source>

```yaml
groups:
- name: example
  rules:

  # Alert for any instance that is unreachable for >5 minutes.

    expr: up == 0
    for: 5m
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "Instance {{ $labels.instance }} down"
      description: "{{ $labels.instance }} of job {{ $labels.job }} has been down for more than 5 minutes."

    expr: api_http_request_latencies_second{quantile="0.5"} > 1
    for: 10m
    annotations:

```
</source>

Silences are configured in the web interface of the Alertmanager.

### Silence Creation and Updates

When a silence is created or updated on any instance:

1. **Local storage** - Silence is stored in the local state map
2. **Broadcast** - Silence is serialized (protobuf) and broadcast via gossip
3. **Merge on receive** - Other instances receive and merge the silence:
   ```go
   // Merge logic: last-write-wins based on UpdatedAt timestamp
   if !exists || incoming.UpdatedAt > existing.UpdatedAt {
       accept_update()
   }
   ```

</source>

### Single Pane of Glass

Users can interact with any Alertmanager instance in the cluster:
- **View silences** - All instances have the same silence state (eventually consistent)
- **Create/update silences** - Changes made on any instance propagate to all peers
- **Delete silences** - Implemented as "expire immediately" + gossip

This provides a unified operational experience regardless of which instance you access.
</source>

These goals prioritize operational reliability and alert delivery over strict exactly-once semantics.

Based on the company's PostgreSQL documentation, here's how to measure replication lag between a Postgres standby and its primary:

## Measuring Replication Lag

You can calculate the replication lag by comparing the WAL (Write-Ahead Log) locations on both servers:

| Source | Function | Location |
|--------|----------|----------|
| **Primary** | `pg_current_wal_lsn()` | Current WAL write position |
| **Standby** | `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()` | Last WAL position received |

### Steps:
1. Run `pg_current_wal_lsn()` on the primary server
2. Run `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()` on the standby server
3. Compare the two positions - the difference represents your replication lag

### Alternative Methods:
- The WAL receive location is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process when using the `ps` command
- You can view real-time replication info via the `pg_stat_replication` view

### Example Query:
```sql
SELECT 
    'primary' as server_type,
    current_setting('log_temp_files', '0') || pg_current_wal_lsn() as wal_lsn;
```

This same approach was identified during Incident INC-2093, where the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary and no monitoring system alerted on the lag [D11:2].

### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

#### Monitoring

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. You can calculate this lag by comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby. These locations can be retrieved using `pg_current_wal_lsn` on the primary and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby, respectively (see section functions-admin-backup-table and section functions-recovery-info-table for details). The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process, displayed using the `ps` command (see section monitoring-ps for details).

#### Planning for High Availability

When a standby first attaches to the primary, it will not yet be properly synchronized. This is described as `catchup` mode. Once the lag between standby and primary reaches zero for the first time we move to real-time `streaming` state. The catch-up duration may be long immediately after the standby has been created. If the standby is shut down, then the catch-up period will increase according to the length of time the standby has been down. The standby is only able to become a synchronous standby once it has reached `streaming` state. This state can be viewed using the pg_stat_replication view.
</source>

### Handling Query Conflicts

g replication.

In a standby server that exists primarily for high availability, it's best to set the delay parameters relatively short, so that the server cannot fall far behind the primary due to delays caused by standby queries. However, if the standby server is meant for executing long-running queries, then a high or even infinite delay value may be preferable. Keep in mind however that a long-running query could cause other sessions on the standby server to not see recent changes on the primary, if it delays application of WAL records.

**To monitor replication lag:**

1. **On the primary server**, check the current WAL write location using:
   ```sql
   SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

As noted in incident INC-2093, replication lag should be monitored closely since standbys can fall significantly behind if not properly watched ([D11:2]).

Based on the company documentation, here's how to measure how far a Postgres standby is behind the primary:

## Measuring Replication Lag

You can measure the replication distance by comparing Log Sequence Numbers (LSN):

**On the primary server:**
```sql
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
```
This returns the current WAL write location.

**On the standby server:**
```sql
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```
This returns the last WAL location received by the standby.

## Calculating the Lag

To calculate the actual lag in terms of bytes or time, you need to compare these two LSN values:

- **Primary**: Get `pg_current_wal_lsn()` 
- **Standby**: Get `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()`

The difference between these two LSN values tells you how many WAL records are in flight (not yet applied on the standby).

## Alternative Method

The last WAL receive location is also visible in the process status of the WAL receiver process using the `ps` command:
```bash
ps aux | grep postgres
```

## Additional Context

For monitoring and alerting purposes, an important health indicator of streaming replication is exactly this amount of WAL records generated in the primary but not yet applied in the standby. You can use views like `pg_stat_replication` to query this information for more detailed metrics including the catchup status and latency measurements [D11:2][46].

## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).
</source>

## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).

Based on the Prometheus documentation, **you should generally use `rate()` for alerts**, not `irate()`. Here's why:

## Key Recommendation

According to the Prometheus query functions documentation [D07:2]:

> **"Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read."**

## When to Use Each

| Metric Type | Recommended Function | Reason |
|-------------|---------------------|--------|
| **Alerts** | `rate()` | Brief changes won't cause false positives that trigger alerts prematurely; more stable readings prevent alert fatigue |
| **Fast-moving counters / Volatile metrics** | `irate()` | Captures rapid spikes better when just monitoring |
| **Slower-moving or steady counters** | `rate()` | More accurate for detecting sustained issues |

## Important Considerations

1. **Counter Resets**: Both functions handle counter resets, but `irate()` relies only on the last two data points, making it more sensitive to noise during restarts.

2. **Graphing vs Alerting**: 
   - Use `irate()` when creating dashboards where you want to visualize rare but important spikes
   - Use `rate()` for alert thresholds to avoid triggering too often due to transient fluctuations

3. **Order of Operations**: Remember, "First the rate, then aggregate" — always apply `rate()` or `irate()` before aggregation operations like `sum()` [D07:3].

In summary: **use `rate()` for your alerting rules** to maintain stability and avoid unnecessary alerts, and save `irate()` for visualization purposes.

Based on the Prometheus documentation, **you should generally use `rate()` for alerts**, not `irate()`. Here's why:

## Key Recommendation

According to the Prometheus query functions documentation [D07:2]:

> **"Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read."**

## When to Use Each

| Metric Type | Recommended Function | Reason |
|-------------|---------------------|--------|
| **Alerts** | `rate()` | Brief changes won't cause false positives that trigger alerts prematurely; more stable readings prevent alert fatigue |
| **Fast-moving counters / Volatile metrics** | `irate()` | Captures rapid spikes better when just monitoring |
| **Slower-moving or steady counters** | `rate()` | More accurate for detecting sustained issues |

## Important Considerations

1. **Counter Resets**: Both functions handle counter resets, but `irate()` relies only on the last two data points, making it more sensitive to noise during restarts.

2. **Graphing vs Alerting**: 
   - Use `irate()` when creating dashboards where you want to visualize rare but important spikes
   - Use `rate()` for alert thresholds to avoid triggering too often due to transient fluctuations

3. **Order of Operations**: Remember, "First the rate, then aggregate" — always apply `rate()` or `irate()` before aggregation operations like `sum()` [D07:3].

In summary: **use `rate()` for your alerting rules** to maintain stability and avoid unnecessary alerts, and save `irate()` for visualization purposes.

- `irate()` calculates the per-second rate using only the last two data points, making it more sensitive to brief fluctuations

Here's why:

> **Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read.**

  expr: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 100
  for: 5m
}

# Not recommended for alerts - too volatile
alert(http_request_irate_high) {
  expr: irate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 100
  for: 5m
}
```

For graphing fast-changing metrics where you need the most recent instant rate, then use `irate()` for visualization purposes instead.

answers:
You get one notification instead of hundreds due to **grouping** in Alertmanager. When many systems fail simultaneously, Prometheus sends hundreds of alerts, but Alertmanager groups them into single notifications based on similarity.

From the Alertmanager documentation [D07:2], grouping "categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification" and is "especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously."

For example, if dozens or hundreds of service instances can't reach their database during a network partition, each instance would trigger an alert. Instead, Alertmanager groups these alerts by the underlying issue and sends just one grouped notification.

This prevents alert fatigue by reducing noise during large-scale incidents while still ensuring you get notified about what's happening.

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager > Grouping" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/notifications.md:4" doc="alertmanager/notifications.md" title="Notification template reference" section="Notification template reference > Alert" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Alert

`Alert` holds one alert for notification templates.

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:8" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Metamonitoring" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Metamonitoring

It is important to have confidence that monitoring is working. Accordingly, have
alerts to ensure that Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, PushGateways, and
other monitoring infrastructure are available and running correctly.

As always, if it is possible to alert on symptoms rather than causes, this helps
to reduce noise. For example, a blackbox test that alerts are getting from
PushGateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than individual
alerts on each.

Supplementing the whitebox monitoring of Prometheus with external blackbox
monitoring can catch problems that are otherwise invisible, and also serves as
a fallback in case internal systems completely fail.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md:8" doc="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md" title="Alerting rules" section="Alerting rules > Sending alert notifications" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Sending alert notifications

Prometheus's alerting rules are good at figuring what is broken *right now*, but
they are not a fully-fledged notification solution. Another layer is needed to
add summarization, notification rate limiting, silencing and alert dependencies
on top of the simple alert definitions. In Prometheus's ecosystem, the
Alertmanager takes on this
role. Thus, Prometheus may be configured to periodically send information about
alert states to an Alertmanager instance, which then takes care of dispatching
the right notifications.
Prometheus can be configured to automatically discover available
Alertmanager instances through its service discovery integrations.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:4" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

You may need alerts for different types of request if they have different
characteristics, or problems in a low-traffic type of request would be drowned
out by high-traffic requests.

answers:
You get one notification instead of hundreds because **Alertmanager groups similar alerts into a single notification**. This is an intentional design feature!

Here's how it works:

**Grouping by labels**
When you configure Alertmanager with `group_by` settings, it batches alerts that share certain labels into a single notification. For example:
```yaml
# Alerts with these properties are grouped together
cluster: production
service: database
severity: high
```
All those hundreds of individual failures from different service instances matching those criteria are consolidated into one compact notification [D07:4].

**The grouping benefit**
This is especially useful during large outages when hundreds or thousands of systems fail simultaneously. Without grouping, you'd receive overwhelming numbers of notifications; with grouping, you get meaningful information about what happened while still being able to see which specific service instances were affected within the same message [D06:4].

**Example scenario**
If dozens of database instances are down during a network partition, Prometheus sends hundreds of alerts to Alertmanager. With proper grouping configuration, Alertmanager bundles them into a single notification summarizing the issue rather than sending 100+ separate messages [D06:4].

**Customization**
You can control which labels trigger grouping by configuring your routing tree in Alertmanager. Use special values like `...` to disable aggregation entirely if needed [D08:5].

### Behavior During Partition

**In Partition A** (AM-1 alone):
- AM-1 sees itself as position 0
- Waits 0 × timeout = 0 seconds
- Sends notifications (no dedup from AM-2/AM-3)

**In Partition B** (AM-2, AM-3):
- AM-2 is position 0, AM-3 is position 1
- AM-2 waits 0 seconds, sends notification
- AM-3 sees AM-2's notification log entry, deduplicates

**Result**: Duplicate notifications sent (one from Partition A, one from Partition B)

This is **intentional** - Alertmanager prefers duplicate notifications over missed alerts.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:16" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Split-Brain Handling (Fail Open)" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Split-Brain Handling (Fail Open)

During a network partition, the cluster may split into multiple groups that cannot communicate. Alertmanager's "fail open" design ensures alerts are still delivered:
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:39" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Troubleshooting > Debug duplicate notifications" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Debug duplicate notifications

Duplicate notifications can occur due to:

1. **Network partitions** (expected, fail-open)
2. **Gossip not settled** - Check `--cluster.settle-timeout`
3. **Clock skew** - Ensure NTP is configured on all instances
4. **Notification log not replicating** - Check gossip metrics

Enable debug logging:

```bash
alertmanager --log.level=debug
```

Look for:
- `"Waiting for gossip to settle..."`
- `"gossip settled; proceeding"`
- Deduplication decisions in notification pipeline
</source>

can no longer reach the database.

### `<route>`

[ receiver: <string> ]
# The labels by which incoming alerts are grouped together. For example,
# multiple alerts coming in for cluster=A and alertname=LatencyHigh would
# be batched into a single group.

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:26" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Prometheus Configuration" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Prometheus Configuration

**Important**: Configure Prometheus to send alerts to **all** Alertmanager instances, not via a load balancer.

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets:
            - am-1.example.com:9093
            - am-2.example.com:9093
            - am-3.example.com:9093
```

This ensures:
- **Redundancy** - If one Alertmanager is down, others still receive alerts
- **Independent processing** - Each instance independently evaluates routing, grouping, and deduplication
- **No single point of failure** - Load balancers introduce a single point of failure
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:6" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Batch jobs" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Batch jobs

For batch jobs it makes sense to page if the batch job has not succeeded
recently enough, and this will cause user-visible problems.

This should generally be at least enough time for 2 full runs of the batch job.
For a job that runs every 4 hours and takes an hour, 10 hours would be a
reasonable threshold. If you cannot withstand a single run failing, run the
job more frequently, as a single failure should not require human intervention.
</source>

You get one notification instead of hundreds because **Alertmanager groups similar alerts into a single notification**. This is an intentional design feature!

Here's how it works:

**Grouping by labels**
When you configure Alertmanager with `group_by` settings, it batches alerts that share certain labels into a single notification. For example:
```yaml
# Alerts with these properties are grouped together
cluster: production
service: database
severity: high
```
All those hundreds of individual failures from different service instances matching those criteria are consolidated into one compact notification [D07:4].

**The grouping benefit**
This is especially useful during large outages when hundreds or thousands of systems fail simultaneously. Without grouping, you'd receive overwhelming numbers of notifications; with grouping, you get meaningful information about what happened while still being able to see which specific service instances were affected within the same message [D06:4].

**Example scenario**
If dozens of database instances are down during a network partition, Prometheus sends hundreds of alerts to Alertmanager. With proper grouping configuration, Alertmanager bundles them into a single notification summarizing the issue rather than sending 100+ separate messages [D06:4].

**Customization**
You can control which labels trigger grouping by configuring your routing tree in Alertmanager. Use special values like `...` to disable aggregation entirely if needed [D08:5].

Here's how it works:

**What is Inhibition?**
Inhibition is a concept that suppresses notifications for certain alerts if other alerts are already firing. This prevents you from getting overwhelmed with hundreds of notifications for related issues.

If your entire cluster becomes unreachable (a single high-level alert fires), Alertmanager can be configured to mute all other individual node alerts concerning that cluster. ### Debug duplicate notifications

Duplicate notifications can occur due to:

1. **Network partitions** (expected, fail-open)
2. **Gossip not settled** - Check `--cluster.settle-timeout`
3. **Clock skew** - Ensure NTP is configured on all instances
4. **Notification log not replicating** - Check gossip metrics

Enable debug logging:

```bash
alertmanager --log.level=debug
```

Look for:
- `"Waiting for gossip to settle..."`
- `"gossip settled; proceeding"`
- Deduplication decisions in notification pipeline
</source>

## Sending alert notifications

Prometheus's alerting rules are good at figuring what is broken *right now*, but
they are not a fully-fledged notification solution. Another layer is needed to

on top of the simple alert definitions. In Prometheus's ecosystem, the
Alertmanager takes on this
role. Thus, Prometheus may be configured to periodically send information about
alert states to an Alertmanager instance, which then takes care of dispatching
the right notifications.

<source id="D04:0" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > What the platform is" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## What the platform is

The agent platform is the set of services our agents run on. Agents are configured in the registry, look things up through shared services, and are watched by monitoring. This page describes the core services and how they connect. It doesn't cover every service an individual agent uses; each agent's owner documents those.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/configuration.md:70" doc="alertmanager/configuration.md" title="Configuration" section="Configuration > General receiver-related settings > `<http_config>` (Shared)" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### `<http_config>` (Shared)

An `http_config` allows configuring the HTTP client that the receiver uses to
communicate with HTTP-based API services.
</source>

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent <agent_name> --scope <scope>
```

**Parameters:**
- `--agent`: The name of the agent to generate a key for (e.g., "support_agent")

content.content:
<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

answers:
Based on the registry documentation [D06:1], the `regctl` command to issue a new key is:

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent <agent_name> --scope <scope>
```

**Parameters:**
- `--agent`: The agent's name (e.g., `support_agent`)
- `--scope`: Either `read` or `write`
  - `read`: Can call every GET endpoint
  - `write`: Can also create, update and delete agents

**Important notes:**
- `regctl` prints the new key once, so you must store it in the secrets manager immediately - it cannot be shown again
- Keys have a scope that determines what actions they're authorized for
- The old key continues to work after issuing a new one, so there's no interruption

**Example:**
```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```
